label: HMRC update · 17 November 2026
title: Self Assessment scams: how to spot a fake HMRC message before 31 January
summary: HMRC has had 1,704 reports of Self Assessment scams in the last 12 months. Here is how the fake refund scams work and what HMRC will never do.
body:
On 17 November 2026 HMRC warned Self Assessment customers to stay alert to scams in the run-up to the 31 January deadline. In the 12 months to 31 October it received 1,704 reports of Self Assessment-related scams, out of 95,340 reports of suspected scams in total.

What the scammers are doing

Fraudsters know that January is when people expect to hear from HMRC. In August 2026 alone, HMRC received around 900 reports linked to a single scam. It used emails with a malicious attachment that led to a fake GOV.UK page. Victims were told they had an unclaimed tax refund and asked to confirm their identity and payment details, which could then be used to get into their bank accounts.

What HMRC will never do

  • Contact you by email, text or phone to tell you that you are due a refund, or ask you to claim one.
  • Ask for personal or financial information by email or text message.
  • Leave threatening voicemails about legal action or arrest.

What I would do

  • Never click a link in a message about a tax refund. Log in to your HMRC online account or the HMRC app directly instead. Any genuine refund will show there.
  • Check before you act. GOV.UK has a page that lists genuine HMRC contact, so you can check whether a message is real.
  • Report it. Forward suspicious emails to phishing@hmrc.gov.uk and texts to 60599. Phone calls can be reported on GOV.UK.
  • Let your accountant be the filter. If we act for you, forward anything that looks like it came from HMRC and we will tell you whether it is genuine.

The deadline to file your 2025 to 2026 return and pay any tax owed is 31 January 2027. Filing early leaves less room for a scammer to catch you in a rush.
